In line with the July 26, 2017 FOMC statement, incoming data continue to indicate a solid labor market and moderate real activity alongside below-2 percent 12-month inflation. A gradual, expectations-consistent policy path remains appropriate, and the planned, cautious start to balance sheet normalization should help avoid disruptive credit-supply effects.

SLOOS perspective: Credit conditions are mixed and modestly less supportive than the macro tone alone suggests. Domestic banks reported weaker demand across CRE (including construction, land development, and multifamily) and consumer credit (auto and credit card), with standards tightened for consumer, auto, and credit card loans. Residential real estate lending standards eased somewhat (including jumbo, QM, and GSE), with home-purchase and HELOC standards broadly unchanged, providing some offset via housing. Demand for nonfarm nonresidential loans was unchanged. Foreign banks reported tighter lending standards across C&I (for small, middle-market, and large firms) and CRE, even as they noted strengthened CRE demand. Net, SLOOS implies a slightly negative credit impulse for consumers and parts of business investment, not a broad-based tightening.

Financial stability considerations remain moderate overall but feature elevated valuation pressures and higher business leverage; combined with the SLOOS softening in credit demand and selective tightening in standards, these factors counsel continued gradualism and a somewhat more guarded stance.

Bottom line: Growth and employment prospects are still cautiously positive, but the SLOOS points to modest headwinds from softer loan demand and tighter consumer credit standards, warranting a slightly lower assessment than before.
